scenarios.scenario_description: Two balloons are filled with equal amounts of gas; one with Helium, one with Argon. Both are kept in a room at constant temperature. A student argues that because the temperature is the same, the particles in both balloons must be moving at the exact same speed.
scenarios.key_insight: Temperature determines the *average Kinetic Energy*, not the speed directly. Since KE depends on mass ($1/2 mv^2$), lighter particles (Helium) must move faster than heavier particles (Argon) to maintain the same energy.
discrimination_factors: Understanding the inverse relationship between mass and speed at constant energy

scenarios.scenario_description: A diffusion experiment is conducted with Gas X and Gas Y. Gas Y is detected 4 times faster than Gas X. Students are asked to determine the ratio of the molar masses of the gases ($M_X / M_Y$) assuming constant temperature.
scenarios.key_insight: Relates Time ($t$) to Speed ($v$) and Speed to Mass ($m$). If Gas Y is faster ($v_y = 4v_x$), then $KE_y = 16 KE_x$ (incorrect logic) OR $v^2 \propto 1/m$. Since $v \propto 1/\sqrt{m}$, a speed ratio of 4 implies a mass ratio of $4^2 = 16$. Gas X is 16 times heavier than Gas Y.
discrimination_factors: Squaring ratios to solve for mass

scenarios.scenario_description: A flask of gas is heated from 300 K to 600 K. A student claims that the particles will travel exactly twice as fast at the higher temperature.
scenarios.key_insight: Kinetic energy is directly proportional to temperature ($T \propto v^2$). Therefore, doubling the temperature (in Kelvin) doubles the KE, which means speed only increases by a factor of $\sqrt{2}$.
discrimination_factors: Understanding the square root relationship between T and v
